planted. You could not blame anyone for that. There was no experience in growing fruit in those areas prior to the early days of this century. Many unsuitable varieties of fruit depressed the market of the fruit growers in general. The fruit growers' association, with the co-operation of the growers, did what they could to eliminate unsuitable varieties.
The fruit growers in British Columbia have done their best to explore every possible market and to overcome the difficulties created by present currency restrictions. In the last few years they have conducted an all-out sales effort led by men who have had long experience in the fruit industry-I should say an international experience in the fruit industry-and are capable of facing every problem they have to meet to the best advantage.
To illustrate that, I think in 1955 some 2.97 per cent of the total receipts from the sale of apples was invested in advertising in that year in an effort to stimulate and increase the market. They have done everything possible to meet changing customs and changing demands on the part of the consumer. They have improved the orthodox packs; they have improved their varieties, and they have also improved their packaging methods. Every avenue along that line has been explored. Therefore I think it is not a question of an industry not exercising restraint running to the government for assistance whenever they get a slight bump or a jar, but it is the representations of the fruit growers of British Columbia, of a group of men and women, of growers, who have indicated they are willing to stand on their own feet and do everything possible within their control.
To illustrate the restraint that the growers of British Columbia have exercised throughout the years in their applications to the federal government, or to other governments, for assistance, I want to give the house this information. The total assistance to the British Columbia fruit industry over the period 1941 to 1954, inclusive, has amounted to $3,622,807.17. During the same period a total of 84,359,621 boxes of apples were produced. The amount of assistance rendered this industry by the government during this period -I am speaking now of the federal government-amounted, therefore, to .0429 cents per bushel. I challenge the minister to give an illustration of any other section of agriculture in Canada that has had as little assistance in comparison with the total value of the crop produced.
I mention these facts, Mr. Speaker, because it is very easy to underestimate their

difficulties, and easy for some people without any knowledge of the fruit growers' experience to say that they come running to the government for assistance without having made every effort possible to assist themselves. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I support the hon. member for Kamloops in his plea to the government to give favourable consideration to any representations the British Columbia fruit growers' association may make on behalf of the tree fruit growers of the interior of British Columbia.
I might mention before I conclude that the fruit growers of British Columbia represent the only section of the agricultural industry in Canada that during the war, because of the shortage of crop on occasions, the tremendous demand and the increased purchasing power as a result of war activities, willingly recommended prices for certain crops such as cherries and soft fruits to the government under the wartime prices control board which were lower than could have been obtained if they had just allowed the competition for their goods to exist in Canada generally.
I think, Mr. Speaker, they have exercised every restraint. They have particular and unique problems as compared with some other sections of agriculture, and because of what they have tried to do for themselves to build up in British Columbia one of the finest marketing organizations in the world, when they are faced with problems over which they have little control this government should give their representations serious and, I trust, favourable consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words to the grievance raised by the hon. member for Kamloops. The growers of the Okanagan -and I am speaking largely of the apple growers-are facing a serious situation, as was mentioned, owing to severe weather conditions which damaged their trees in the winters of 1953-54 and 54-55. As a result, in 1955 they produced a very small crop owing to the weakened condition of the trees. The crop was small in quantity and it was also not so good in quality, which is unusual for Okanagan products.
I can also assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the British Columbia growers are not in the habit of coming hat in hand to this government for financial assistance; but owing to conditions beyond their control in 1955 they were saddled with tremendous losses in their operations. On the average they received a price of 76 cents per box for the top grade apples.
It is estimated, Mr. Speaker, that it costs $1.25 to produce top grade apples in the 
Okanagan valley. The lower grades, of course, C's and culls, are dealt with in other ways. They have their own methods of taking care of these by processing them into apple juice, canned apple sauce and dry materials. Therefore they are concerned mainly with the top grades, or the fancy dessert apples which have made a name for themselves throughout Canada.
As I say, they realized the sum of 76 cents a box for these apples in 1955. I understand they have made a plea to this government, and they have been advised that the maximum they can obtain is 40 cents a box. Since they have already received 76 cents, they are away over and above what this government considers it should cost to raise a box of apples.
I believe anyone with any sense will laugh at the idea that you can produce a box of apples today for 40 cents. The insistence of the prices support board on retaining that ridiculously low floor price, if I may describe it as such, indicates that they are certainly not taking a realistic view of existing conditions.
I understand that these growers have already contacted this government and have asked that the price they received of 76 cents a box be supplemented from the funds which are in the hands of the prices support board to give them at least sufficient money to continue producing and endeavour under very difficult circumstances to build up their orchards by replanting some of the trees that had been completely destroyed, in order to carry on in the future with some degree of success. In view of the treatment these growers have received in their modest appeals for assistance in the past, and in view of their courage and determination to carry on in the future with a minimum of assistance, I would strongly urge that the Minister of Agriculture and the officials of his department give every sympathetic consideration to their plea for financial assistance in compensating for the difficult years they have just experienced.
